opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I tried not to present myself as the expert, because nobody really is one yet. OpenClaw moved so fast that whatever I'd have claimed as authority would've been out of date by the time the slides were exported. So I framed it as, "I'm someone who's been living with this thing day to day, breaking it, fixing it, and here's what I've learned." More practitioner than professor.

I also leaned into my own setup pretty heavily: I showed what my agent actually does for me, where it's genuinely useful, and where it embarrassed me. I think people trust you more when you show the failure cases alongside the cool demos. If you only show the highlight reel, the audience assumes you're selling something.

And because a lot of the room was students, I wanted them to walk out feeling like they could go build this themselves that night. So less "look how smart I am," more "here's the map, here are the sharp edges, go play." That felt like the honest way to do it given how early we all are.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he avoided presenting himself as an expert and focused on his day-to-day setup, lessons, and demos; it does not attribute that choice to discussing the architecture.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the main thing I did was get out of my own way. I'm not the OpenClaw guy. I didn't write the thing, I'm not on the core team, and I think if I'd walked in trying to present as the expert, people would've smelled it immediately. So I framed it very explicitly as "here's someone who's spent a lot of hours actually using this, breaking it, and reading the code when the docs ran out." That's a more honest position and, frankly, it's the position most people in the room were also in. They weren't there to hear a product pitch, they wanted to know what it actually feels like to build with it.

The second thing was that I tried to lead with the mental model rather than the feature list. Anyone can read the README. What's harder to get is the "why is it shaped this way" part, the design decisions that only make sense once you've hit the wall they were built to avoid. So a lot of the talk was me saying, here's a mistake I made, here's what the framework was quietly trying to stop me from doing, and here's the thing I eventually understood. That turned out to be the right register, because people kept nodding at the mistakes, not at the slides.

And then I kept a pretty strict rule for myself about not overclaiming. If I wasn't sure how something worked internally, I said so. I'd rather someone leave thinking "he was useful and knew his limits" than "he said something confident that I later found out was wrong." In this space the half-life of confident claims is about three weeks anyway.

r001.rationale: He says he avoided presenting as an expert and focused on the framework’s mental model and design decisions, but does not attribute his limited self-presentation to discussing its architecture.

astra-6.text: I wanted to come across as someone thinking through the material alongside the audience. The goal was to make my reasoning clear—what I understood, what assumptions I was making, and where I was still uncertain—and give people room to question it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes presenting his reasoning and inviting questions, but does not attribute limited self-presentation to a focus on discussing the architecture.

sol-6.1.text: I tried to present myself as a fellow builder—someone working through the ideas alongside the audience. I wanted to make my reasoning visible: what I was trying to do, why I made certain choices, and where I was still uncertain. Hopefully that makes the lecture feel more like an invitation to explore than a polished set of answers.
